passages.text: New to yoga or coming back after a long break? Willow Lane Yoga, the small studio above the corner bakery on Hart Street, is opening its doors to the neighborhood this month. Our classes are capped at twelve people, so instructors can give every student personal attention, and mats and blocks are provided free of charge. Morning, lunchtime, and evening sessions fit around any schedule. To welcome new members, we are offering 50 percent off your first month of unlimited classes. Just sign up before the end of the month and ____.

Is your old bicycle gathering dust in the garage because of a flat tire or a squeaky chain? Spokes & Gears Community Garage is holding a hands-on repair workshop every Saturday morning in November. Our volunteer mechanics will show you how to patch tubes, adjust brakes, and replace worn chains, and then you do the work with your own hands. We also sell refurbished secondhand bikes at fair prices, and every one has been inspected for safety. Bring your own bike along, and by the end of the session, ____.

____. Along the principal highways of their empire, the Romans erected tall stone columns at regular intervals, each inscribed with the distance to the nearest settlement or back to Rome itself. The Roman mile was reckoned as a thousand paces of a marching legionary, a unit that gave these markers their name: milestones. For merchants, couriers, and armies alike, the columns made it feasible to plan an itinerary and estimate its duration. Many survive today, and the word has endured as a metaphor for any significant juncture of progress.

____. Its creator, L. L. Zamenhof, grew up in a city where Polish, Russian, German, and Yiddish speakers coexisted but often harbored mutual suspicion. He was convinced that much of this hostility stemmed from people's inability to comprehend one another. In the late nineteenth century, he published a language with simple, regular grammar and virtually no exceptions, hoping it could function as a neutral auxiliary language for all. Because it belonged to no single nation, no ethnic group would gain an advantage by adopting it.

When offices emptied during the transition to remote work, the repercussions extended far beyond the companies themselves. Downtown delicatessens, dry cleaners, and parking garages had long depended on the steady influx of commuters who arrived each weekday morning. With many employees now working from home several days a week, these businesses saw their weekday clientele plummet. Some closed permanently, while others curtailed their hours or relocated closer to residential areas. Meanwhile, cafes in suburban neighborhoods reported busier lunchtimes than ever. In short, remote work did not diminish spending so much as ____.

____. When employees must actively enroll in a retirement savings plan, many never get around to it, even if they intend to save. But when companies enroll workers automatically and allow them to opt out, participation rises dramatically. The available options are identical in both cases; only the starting point differs. Economists call this the default effect: people tend to adhere to whatever option is preselected for them, whether out of inertia, procrastination, or a tacit assumption that the preset choice must be the recommended one.

____. Proponents argue that tipping rewards attentive service and gives servers a chance to earn more than a fixed wage would permit. Critics, however, contend that it renders workers' income volatile and shifts the burden of compensating staff from employers to customers. Some studies also suggest that the size of a gratuity depends less on the quality of service than on extraneous factors such as the weather or the server's appearance. Consequently, a growing number of restaurants have replaced tipping with higher menu prices and fixed wages.

As single-person households multiply, grocery chains and food manufacturers are reconsidering what they sell. A family-sized sack of potatoes or a whole watermelon makes little sense for someone cooking only for one, and much of it ends up being discarded. In response, supermarkets now stock half cabbages, single servings of meat, and soups in containers designed for one meal. Convenience stores have likewise expanded their assortments of individually packaged side dishes. For these retailers, the lesson is unmistakable: in a society of smaller households, ____.

The octopus is a consummate master of camouflage. Specialized cells in its skin, called chromatophores, allow it to change color in a fraction of a second, and it can raise minute protrusions on its skin to mimic the texture of rocks or seaweed. What makes this ability so perplexing is that most octopuses are believed to be colorblind, possessing only one type of photoreceptor in their eyes. ____, they somehow manage to match the hues of their surroundings with remarkable fidelity. Scientists are still investigating the mechanism, and some speculate that their skin itself may be able to detect light.

Birds inhabiting cities face a challenge that their rural counterparts do not: incessant noise. Traffic, construction, and machinery generate a persistent low-pitched rumble that can drown out birdsong. To make themselves audible, many urban birds have modified their songs. Researchers comparing urban and woodland populations of the same species have found that city birds often sing at a noticeably higher pitch. ____, their songs rise above the frequencies dominated by traffic, allowing mates and rivals to discern them more clearly. Some species also sing earlier in the morning, before the rush hour commences.

The margins of medieval manuscripts are often filled with bizarre images. (a) Most manuscripts were written on parchment, which was fashioned from meticulously prepared animal hides. (b) Alongside solemn religious texts, scribes and illuminators drew knights battling giant snails, rabbits hunting people, and monkeys playing instruments. (c) Scholars still debate why these incongruous scenes appear, suggesting that they may have been jokes, moral allegories, or simply a means of relieving tedium. (d) Whatever their purpose, the drawings offer a rare glimpse of the humor and imagination of the artisans who produced the books.

Bike-sharing schemes have become a ubiquitous sight in cities around the world. (a) Users can unlock a bicycle with a smartphone app, ride it across town, and leave it at another docking station near their destination. (b) For short trips, this is often quicker than waiting for a bus and cheaper than hailing a taxi. (c) Professional cyclists, by contrast, usually train on lightweight racing bikes that can cost thousands of dollars. (d) Municipal officials also hope the schemes will mitigate traffic congestion and encourage residents to exercise more.

During this period, all due dates will be automatically extended until March 20, and no late fees will be charged. The book drop outside the main entrance will remain open, but returned items will not be checked in until we reopen. Patrons can still borrow e-books and audiobooks through our website. We apologize for any inconvenience.

Building Management Office

Now Hiring: Part-Time Baristas
Corner Cup Cafe is looking for friendly, reliable baristas to join our team for weekend shifts. No prior experience is necessary, as all new staff will complete a two-week paid training program covering coffee preparation, food safety, and customer service. Applicants must be available on both Saturdays and Sundays and able to work early morning hours. Staff enjoy free drinks during shifts and a discount on all menu items. To apply, drop off your resume at the counter or email it to our manager.

I never thought of myself as a runner. Two years ago, I could barely jog to the end of my street without stopping. But after a friend talked me into joining a beginners' running club, I slowly built up my distance, week by week. Last Sunday, I crossed the finish line of my first marathon. My time was far from impressive, and I walked for parts of the last few miles, but that didn't matter. What I learned is that big goals rarely require extraordinary talent, only small steps taken consistently.

Dear Hannah,
My roommate and I have shared an apartment for a year, and we used to get along well. Lately, though, she leaves dirty dishes in the sink for days and has friends over late on weeknights when I need to sleep. I've dropped hints, but nothing has changed. How can I fix this without ruining our friendship?
- Tired in Toledo

Dear Tired,
Hints are easy to miss. Choose a calm moment and tell her directly how these habits affect you. Then suggest a few simple house rules that you can both agree on.

Kabuki, one of Japan's most renowned theatrical forms, is famous today for its all-male casts. Yet the genre was actually pioneered in the early seventeenth century by a woman, Izumo no Okuni, whose exuberant dance performances in Kyoto drew large crowds. Female troupes soon flourished, but the ruling shogunate, concerned that the shows fostered immoral conduct, barred women from the stage. Adolescent boys assumed their roles until they, too, were prohibited for similar reasons. Adult male actors then became the norm, and some specialized in portraying female characters, a role known as onnagata.

Most world maps displayed in classrooms are based on a projection devised by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in the sixteenth century. Mercator designed his map for mariners: any straight line drawn on it represents a constant compass bearing, which made navigation considerably simpler. To achieve this, however, the map must enlarge areas progressively the farther they lie from the equator. Consequently, Greenland appears roughly comparable in size to Africa, even though Africa is in fact more than ten times larger. Territories near the poles thus look far more expansive than they really are.

In negotiations, the first figure mentioned often exerts a disproportionate influence on the final outcome. This phenomenon, known as anchoring, occurs because people tend to adjust their estimates from an initial reference point, and they seldom adjust sufficiently. A seller who opens with an exorbitant price, for example, can pull the buyer's counteroffer upward, even if the buyer recognizes the opening figure as unrealistic. For this reason, many negotiation experts advise making the first offer yourself, provided you have ascertained what a reasonable price would be.

Streaming video, music, cloud storage, meal kits, fitness apps: for many consumers, monthly subscriptions have quietly proliferated. Each one seems affordable in isolation, but cumulatively they can amount to a substantial monthly bill. Analysts have coined the term "subscription fatigue" to describe the exasperation people feel as they struggle to keep track of what they pay for. One widespread grievance is that cancelling is often far more cumbersome than signing up, requiring phone calls or several bewildering steps. As a result, some consumers now audit their subscriptions every few months and terminate those they rarely use.

Under a deposit-return scheme, shoppers pay a small surcharge when they buy a beverage in a plastic bottle or can. When they bring the empty container back to a store or a reverse vending machine, the deposit is refunded. Because the money is reimbursed only if the container comes back, people have a tangible incentive not to throw it away, and when some do discard containers, others often collect them for the refund. Jurisdictions that have adopted such schemes typically see much higher return rates, and the collected containers are cleaner and easier to recycle than those retrieved from mixed household waste.

As populations age, many countries are debating whether elderly drivers should face more stringent license renewal requirements. Advocates of tougher rules point out that eyesight, reflexes, and judgment can deteriorate with age, and they call for mandatory vision and cognitive assessments beyond a certain age. Opponents argue that age alone is an unreliable predictor of driving competence and that such rules unfairly target a demographic that, as a whole, is not the most hazardous on the road. They also warn that revoking a license can leave older residents of rural areas isolated, since they may have no alternative means of transportation.

Sleep is not merely a period when the brain shuts down. During deep sleep, the hippocampus, a region implicated in forming new memories, replays patterns of neural activity from the day. These signals appear to facilitate the transfer of information to the brain's outer layer, the cortex, where memories are consolidated for the long term. In experiments, participants who learned a task and then slept performed better the next day than those who remained awake for an equivalent interval. Researchers believe that sleep helps the brain determine which experiences merit retention.

Every year, many migratory birds travel thousands of kilometers and return to the same breeding grounds with astonishing precision. Part of their secret appears to be an ability to perceive Earth's magnetic field. In laboratory experiments, birds placed in cages surrounded by artificial magnetic fields altered the direction in which they attempted to fly when the field was shifted. Scientists hypothesize that certain proteins in the birds' retinas respond to magnetism, possibly enabling them to "see" the field as a pattern superimposed on their vision. Exactly how the signal reaches the brain, however, remains elusive.

Why I Still Keep a Paper Diary
Every night before bed, I open a battered notebook and chronicle my day with a fountain pen. Friends who know me as someone glued to a laptop all day find this ritual oddly anachronistic. Why not simply type notes into a phone app, they ask, where everything can be searched and backed up?
My answer is that handwriting compels me to slow down. Because I cannot write as quickly as I think, I have to decide which thoughts deserve a place on the page. That modest act of selection transforms a jumble of events into something closer to reflection. Several studies have suggested that people who take notes by hand tend to process information more deeply than those who type, and that corroborates my own experience.
There is also something about the physical notebook itself. Leafing through old pages, I can see where my handwriting grew hurried during a stressful month or tidy and relaxed on a holiday. No app has ever given me that. My diary is not efficient, but efficiency was never the point.

Paper is among history's most consequential inventions, yet for centuries it was known only in East Asia. Chinese artisans were manufacturing paper from plant fibers such as hemp and mulberry bark during the Han dynasty, and the technique gradually spread to Korea and Japan. Its westward diffusion, however, was far slower.
According to a well-known anecdote, Chinese papermakers captured during a battle in Central Asia in the eighth century taught their craft in Samarkand. Historians now question whether the story is entirely accurate, but it is evident that papermaking was established in the Islamic world around that time. Baghdad soon had its own paper mills, and officials there swiftly adopted paper in place of parchment and papyrus for administrative records, since it was cheaper and harder to alter without leaving traces.
From the Middle East, the technique migrated across North Africa into Spain, which had paper mills by the twelfth century, and later spread to Italy and the rest of Europe. By the time the printing press emerged in the fifteenth century, Europe had an ample supply of paper, which helped printed books disseminate rapidly.

Can Working Less Mean Accomplishing More?
Over the past several years, dozens of companies in different countries have experimented with a four-day work week, in which employees work four days instead of five without any reduction in pay. The idea sounds like a recipe for diminished productivity, but the preliminary results have surprised many skeptics.
In many of the trials, companies reported that output remained roughly constant. Managers found that staff squandered less time in superfluous meetings and were more focused during the hours they did work. Employees, for their part, described lower stress, better sleep, and more time for family. Several firms also said that the extra day off made it easier to recruit and retain skilled workers.
Still, the model is not a panacea for every workplace. Hospitals, schools, and stores that must remain open daily cannot simply close on Fridays, and they often have to hire additional staff or reconfigure shifts. Critics also note that the companies that volunteered for the trials may have been unusually well suited to them in the first place.

Before booking a hotel or purchasing a new gadget, most shoppers now consult online reviews. That habit has spawned a lucrative market for fraudulent ones. Some businesses pay people to post glowing reviews of their own products, while others publish fabricated complaints about competitors. Specialized firms even sell bundles of five-star ratings written by accounts that have never used the product.
Regulators in several countries have begun to respond. New rules empower authorities to fine companies that buy, sell, or knowingly publish fake reviews, and they also target businesses that suppress negative reviews while displaying only favorable ones. Online platforms, for their part, are deploying algorithms to detect suspicious patterns, such as dozens of near-identical reviews posted within a few hours.
Enforcement remains arduous, however. Fake reviewers increasingly use AI tools to generate text that sounds authentic, and many operate from countries beyond the jurisdiction of local regulators. Consumer advocates therefore advise shoppers to read a range of reviews, including moderate ones, rather than relying on star averages alone.

Artificial light has transformed the nocturnal environment across much of the planet. Streetlights, illuminated billboards, and floodlit buildings now brighten the sky over cities and their suburbs, a phenomenon known as light pollution. For many creatures that are active after dark, this glow is far from innocuous.
Fireflies are particularly vulnerable. Many species rely on rhythmic flashes of light to locate and attract mates, and males and females communicate through precisely timed signals. In brightly lit areas, these faint flashes are obscured by the surrounding glare, so prospective partners struggle to find one another. Researchers have observed that fireflies in illuminated habitats tend to flash less frequently, and some local populations appear to be dwindling as a result.
Migratory birds face a different hazard. Many species travel at night and orient themselves partly by the stars. Brightly lit skyscrapers can disorient them, luring them off course until they circle the buildings in exhaustion or collide with windows. In response, several cities now urge the owners of tall buildings to dim or switch off nonessential lights during peak migration seasons.

Have you always aspired to build your own app but never known where to begin? CodeNest Academy offers beginner-friendly online courses taught by practicing developers. Our concise video lessons fit into any schedule, and each unit culminates in a small project you can showcase to friends or prospective employers. Stuck on a problem? Our mentors respond to queries within a day. Best of all, you can sample any course for two weeks without paying a cent. Enroll today and ____.

Tired of supermarket vegetables that were harvested weeks ago? Visit the Maple Square Weekend Market, open every Saturday and Sunday from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. More than forty local growers bring produce picked the day before, along with artisanal bread, wildflower honey, and handmade cheese. Because there are no intermediaries, prices are often lower than in stores, and you can ask the farmers themselves how their crops were cultivated. Bring your own bags, arrive early for the choicest selection, and ____.

In ancient Greek theater, ____. A small cast of actors, often no more than three, was expected to perform every speaking role in a play, including women, deities, and monarchs. By simply swapping masks between scenes, a single actor could embody several distinct characters. The masks also bore exaggerated features that remained recognizable even to spectators seated far from the stage in vast open-air amphitheaters. Because they were typically fashioned from linen, cork, or wood, scarcely any original masks have survived; most of what we know derives from vase paintings and sculptures.

The word 'robot' originated not in a laboratory but on a stage. It first appeared in R.U.R., a 1920 play by the Czech writer Karel Čapek, in which a factory manufactures artificial laborers that eventually revolt against their human masters. Čapek later credited his brother Josef with coining the term, which derived from the Czech word robota, denoting forced labor or drudgery. The play was soon translated into numerous languages, and the neologism spread with it. In other words, a term now associated with cutting-edge engineering ____.

Psychologists have found that ____. In one classic experiment, participants who were given a coffee mug demanded far more money to relinquish it than others were willing to pay to acquire the identical mug. Having owned the item for only a few minutes, the sellers already perceived parting with it as a loss. This tendency, known as loss aversion, helps explain why investors cling to plummeting stocks and why consumers respond more strongly to a 'lose your discount' message than to a 'gain a discount' one.

On a summer afternoon, ____. Asphalt roads, concrete facades, and dark rooftops absorb sunlight during the day and radiate the heat gradually at night, while the scarcity of trees means there is little shade or cooling from evaporation. One increasingly popular remedy is the green roof, a layer of soil and vegetation installed atop a building. The plants shade the surface and release moisture into the air, keeping the roof and the rooms beneath it cooler, and they also absorb rainwater that would otherwise overwhelm storm drains.

When e-readers surged in popularity, many analysts predicted that the printed book would soon go the way of the cassette tape. For a few years, sales of electronic books rose sharply, seemingly vindicating the forecast. Then growth decelerated and plateaued, while print sales held steady and in some genres even rebounded. Surveys suggest that many readers relish the tactile feel of paper, like to display books at home, and crave a respite from screens. For now, it seems, digital and printed books ____.

Online platforms ____. Every click, like, and pause is logged, and recommendation algorithms exploit this data to show more of whatever kept a user watching or reading. The result can be comfortable, but critics warn that it also fosters a 'filter bubble,' in which people seldom encounter views that challenge their own. Over time, a user who mainly sees articles endorsing one opinion may come to believe that nearly everyone shares it. Some platforms now let users reset their recommendations or deliberately inject unfamiliar topics.

Male humpback whales sing long, intricate songs during the breeding season, and all the males in one population usually sing nearly the same version. These songs, however, are not static. Researchers studying whales in the South Pacific found that a novel song would emerge in one population and then be adopted by neighboring groups, propagating across the ocean over a few years until the old song had vanished. ____, the whales seem to be transmitting a cultural trait, much as catchy pop songs spread from one city to another.

Before the mid-nineteenth century, news could travel no faster than the horse, ship, or train that carried it, so reports of distant events often arrived days or even weeks late. The advent of electric telegraphy altered this dramatically. Operators transmitted messages as electrical pulses along wires using Morse code, a system in which each letter is represented by a sequence of short and long signals called dots and dashes. ____, information that once took weeks to cross a continent could arrive within minutes, and newspapers began printing dispatches from faraway cities on the very day events occurred.

Numerous everyday English expressions were first recorded in the celebrated plays of William Shakespeare. (a) Shakespeare's playhouse, the Globe, was reconstructed near its original site in London in the late twentieth century. (b) Characterizing jealousy as a 'green-eyed monster,' for instance, derives from his tragedy Othello. (c) Likewise, a futile pursuit is still dubbed a 'wild-goose chase,' a phrase found in Romeo and Juliet. (d) Because his plays were performed and printed so extensively, such phrases gradually permeated common speech and persist in usage even today.

Several cities have experimented with making public transportation free for everyone. (a) Proponents argue that abolishing fares helps low-income residents reach jobs, schools, and hospitals more readily. (b) Cities that piloted the idea usually saw ridership climb, especially among people who had seldom taken buses before. (c) However, studies suggest that many new riders were former pedestrians or cyclists, so congestion did not abate as much as anticipated. (d) Bus drivers in many countries must pass a rigorous licensing test that includes both written and road examinations.

Harbor City Museum of Natural History: Summer Evening Hours
From July 1 to August 31, the museum will remain open until 9 p.m. every Friday and Saturday. Evening visitors can explore all permanent galleries, but the special dinosaur exhibition will close at 7 p.m. for nightly maintenance. On Saturday evenings only, guided flashlight tours of the Ocean Hall will commence at 8 p.m. Admission is half price after 6 p.m., and tickets can be purchased at the entrance. Members are admitted free at all times.

Dear Ms. Alvarez,

Effective next month, the complimentary checked baggage allowance on economy fares will be reduced from two bags to one, and each bag may weigh no more than 23 kilograms. A second bag can be added online for a fee prior to departure, which costs less than paying at the airport. Your carry-on allowance remains unchanged.
Sincerely,
SkyBridge Customer Service

Lumen Language Services is seeking freelance translators to join our expanding team. We handle documents for clients in law, medicine, and technology, and we currently need translators working from Korean or Japanese into English. Applicants should possess at least three years of professional experience and be comfortable meeting stringent deadlines. All work is conducted remotely, and you can decide how many assignments to accept each month. To apply, submit your résumé and a one-page sample translation via the Careers page on our website.

When I moved into a cramped apartment last spring, I assumed gardening was a pastime I would have to forgo. Then a neighbor gave me a few cherry tomato seedlings, and I set them in pots on my sunny balcony. Within weeks I had added lettuce, basil, and chili peppers. The harvest was never bountiful, but plucking a salad's worth of leaves before dinner felt like a small daily triumph. More than the produce, I cherished the tranquil ten minutes I spent watering each morning. A tiny balcony, I discovered, is ample space for a garden.

Q: I'm 34 and have worked as an accountant for ten years. The pay is good, but I dread Monday mornings. I've always aspired to become a high school teacher, yet I worry it's too late and that my family can't absorb a pay cut. (Stuck in Numbers)
A: It's not too late. Many teachers enter the classroom from other careers, and your aptitude for numbers could make you a formidable math teacher. Before you resign, though, test the idea. Volunteer as a tutor on weekends. Meanwhile, sit down with your family and draft a budget based on a teacher's salary.

The Inca built one of the largest empires in the Americas without any known writing system. Instead, they kept records using khipu (also spelled quipu), bundles of dyed cotton or wool cords knotted at intervals. The type and position of each knot denoted a number, and the system was decimal, based on units of ten. Administrators used khipu to monitor taxes, census tallies, and commodities stored in state storehouses. Some scholars believe khipu also encoded narratives or names, but no one has yet fully deciphered them.

The haiku is a Japanese poetic form renowned for its brevity. A traditional haiku comprises seventeen sound units arranged in three phrases of five, seven, and five. It customarily includes a seasonal word, known as a kigo, such as 'frog' for spring or 'snow' for winter, which situates the poem in a particular time of year. Rather than articulating feelings directly, a haiku presents a single vivid image and leaves readers to intuit the emotion beneath it. The seventeenth-century poet Matsuo Bashō helped elevate the form to a serious art.

Delivery couriers, ride-hailing drivers, and other app-based workers constitute a growing share of the labor force. Platform companies classify most of them as independent contractors rather than employees, so the companies are not obliged to provide paid leave, health insurance, or a guaranteed minimum wage. Companies contend that this arrangement affords workers the flexibility to choose their own hours. Critics retort that many gig workers rely on a single app for their entire livelihood and should be protected accordingly. Several governments are now weighing legislation that would establish an intermediate category with basic benefits.

A smartphone app called PlateSaver is helping restaurants and bakeries curb food waste. Near closing time, shops list items they have not sold that day, and app users can reserve a 'surprise bag' of these items for roughly a third of the usual price. Users do not know precisely what the bag will contain, and they must collect it in person during a designated time window. Shops recoup some of their costs, customers get inexpensive meals, and perfectly edible food stays out of landfills. Apps of this kind have proliferated in many cities.

Economists have long debated why fertility rates are declining in many affluent countries, and housing costs are emerging as one pivotal factor. Studies in several countries have found that when home prices escalate sharply, young couples who rent tend to postpone having children or have fewer of them. Many couples feel they need an extra bedroom before starting a family, and larger dwellings are especially costly. Intriguingly, homeowners sometimes respond in the opposite way: rising prices make them feel wealthier, and their fertility may even show a slight uptick.

A growing number of resorts now offer 'digital detox' packages. Guests surrender their phones and laptops at check-in and spend their stay hiking, cooking, or simply reading by the lake. Paradoxically, these packages often cost more than ordinary stays, yet many sell out months in advance. Organizers say their most loyal patrons are executives and office workers who answer emails late into the night. Several guests concede that the first day feels disorienting, but by the third day they stop instinctively reaching for their pockets.

Laughter is remarkably contagious. Researchers have found that people are far more likely to laugh in the company of others than in solitude, even while watching the same comedy. Neuroimaging studies show that merely hearing someone laugh activates brain regions that prime the facial muscles to smile, as if the listener were preparing to join in. Interestingly, most laughter in daily conversation follows mundane remarks rather than jokes, suggesting that its primary role is social bonding.

Scientists searching for life on Mars face a perplexing problem: the planet's soil may be hostile to the very evidence they seek. Landers have detected salts called perchlorates in the Martian regolith. These compounds are toxic to many organisms, and when soil samples are heated inside a lander's instruments, perchlorates can decompose organic molecules before they are measured. Moreover, the tenuous atmosphere lets intense radiation bombard the surface. For these reasons, many researchers argue that the most promising place to look is in rock beneath the surface.

Not long ago, dining alone at a restaurant was something many people avoided. Patrons sitting by themselves feared being stigmatized as lonely or unpopular, and some establishments even refused to seat solitary customers during peak hours. Today the landscape has changed dramatically. Noodle shops with private booths, counter seating at cafés, and menus offering single portions have made solo dining commonplace in many cities.
Part of the shift is demographic: more people live alone than ever before, and grueling working hours leave scant time to arrange meals with friends. But I believe something more profound is at play. For many of us, a meal alone is no longer a sign of failure but a modest act of self-care. It is an opportunity to savor exactly what we crave, at an unhurried pace, without the obligation of conversation. I often bring a book, and I leave feeling more rejuvenated than after a boisterous group dinner.
Of course, communal meals still matter. Yet a society that embraces solo diners is one that respects personal autonomy, and that is worth celebrating.

When people think of printing with movable metal type, they usually envision Johannes Gutenberg in fifteenth-century Germany. Yet decades before his celebrated Bible, printers in Korea's Goryeo dynasty were already producing books with metal type.
The most compelling evidence is Jikji, an anthology of Buddhist teachings printed at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju in 1377. It is the oldest extant book known to have been printed with movable metal type. Historical records indicate that Goryeo printers had employed metal type even earlier, but no copies of those volumes remain.
Ironically, the sole known surviving copy of Jikji is not in Korea. It was taken to France in the late nineteenth century and is now housed at the National Library of France in Paris. Only the second of its two volumes survives. In 2001, UNESCO inscribed Jikji on its Memory of the World Register, acknowledging its significance in the history of printing. Today, Cheongju operates a museum devoted to early printing, and many Koreans hope the book will one day be exhibited at home.

The European Union has some of the world's most stringent regulations on carbon emissions. Factories inside the EU must buy permits for the carbon dioxide they release, which raises their costs. This creates a risk known as 'carbon leakage': companies may relocate production to countries with laxer rules, or EU buyers may simply import cheaper goods manufactured there. Either way, emissions are not curtailed; they are merely displaced elsewhere.
To tackle this problem, the EU has introduced the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, or CBAM. Under this system, importers of certain carbon-intensive products, such as steel, cement, aluminum, and fertilizers, must pay a levy based on the emissions generated in making those goods. If a producer has already paid a carbon price in its home country, that amount can be deducted.
Proponents say the measure puts domestic and foreign producers on an equal footing and incentivizes other countries to adopt their own carbon pricing. Detractors, especially in developing economies, contend that it functions as a disguised trade barrier and imposes a heavy burden on exporters that lack the capital to adopt cleaner technology.

When clinics shut their doors during the pandemic, many patients consulted their doctors through a screen for the first time. Video appointments, once a niche service, swiftly became routine, and many people discovered they preferred them. Patients in rural areas no longer had to drive for hours to see a specialist, and harried parents could consult a pediatrician without taking a day off work.
Telemedicine is not, however, a flawless substitute for an office visit. Physicians cannot listen to a patient's lungs or palpate a tender abdomen through a camera, so some conditions may be overlooked. Elderly patients, who often need care the most, may struggle with apps or lack dependable internet connections. There are also qualms about privacy when sensitive medical information is transmitted online.
For these reasons, many health experts now favor a hybrid model. Routine check-ins, prescription renewals, and follow-up consultations can be handled remotely, while initial diagnoses and physical examinations remain in person. Used this way, telemedicine can save patients time and free up clinic capacity for those who genuinely need to be seen.

Scientists once regarded the bacteria in our intestines chiefly as aids to digestion. Increasingly, however, researchers suspect that these trillions of microbes also modulate how we feel.
The gut and the brain are linked by the vagus nerve, a long nerve that relays signals in both directions. In addition, gut bacteria help synthesize compounds that act on the nervous system, and much of the body's serotonin, a neurotransmitter associated with mood, is produced in the gut. In experiments, germ-free mice raised without any bacteria reacted to stress differently from ordinary mice. When researchers transplanted gut bacteria from people with depression into rodents, the animals began to exhibit more anxious behavior.
These findings have sparked enthusiasm about 'psychobiotics,' probiotic foods or supplements that might bolster mental health. Yet experts urge caution. Most of the evidence derives from animal studies, and human trials have so far yielded inconsistent results. Diet, sleep, and stress all affect both mood and gut bacteria, making cause and effect difficult to disentangle. For now, eating a varied diet rich in fiber is prudent, but it is no substitute for proven treatments.

Do you feel guilty leaving your dog home alone all day? At Brightpaw Day Care, your furry companion will spend the day frolicking with other dogs under the vigilant eye of our certified trainers. Our spacious indoor play area is sanitized twice daily, and every dog gets a secluded nap corner after lunch. Owners can even check in through live video on their phones. Drop your dog off on your commute and collect a tired, contented companion in the evening. With us, ____.

____. Before the Vikings adopted the Latin alphabet, they inscribed runes, a set of angular characters carved into wood, bone, and stone. Horizontal strokes would have run parallel to the grain of the wood and been nearly invisible, so carvers avoided them and favored vertical and diagonal lines instead. Carving was also laborious, so most surviving runic inscriptions are terse: names of owners, memorials to the deceased, or brief messages. Longer narratives, such as the renowned sagas, were transmitted orally and committed to parchment only centuries later.

____. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the most celebrated stars of Italian opera were castrati, male singers who had been castrated as boys so that their voices would never deepen. As adults, they combined a soprano or alto range with the lung capacity of a grown man, producing a timbre audiences found exhilarating. Composers wrote dazzling heroic roles for them, and the most illustrious could amass fortunes. Today the practice is rightly regarded as barbaric, and those roles are usually performed by women or by countertenors.

Many retailers pledge to match any lower price a customer finds at a rival store. At first glance, such guarantees seem to be a boon to shoppers, since they appear to drive stores into fierce price wars. Economists, however, point out a subtler consequence. If every store promises to match its rivals, no store gains additional customers by slashing its prices, because competitors will simply match the cut. Consequently, the guarantees may eliminate the incentive to compete at all. In this way, a policy that sounds consumer-friendly can paradoxically ____.

____. A decade ago, coworking spaces were patronized mostly by freelancers and fledgling start-ups that could not afford an office lease of their own. Now large corporations rent entire floors in them. Companies say the arrangement lets them add or eliminate desks within weeks instead of committing to ten-year leases, and it allows staff to work closer to home in branches dispersed across the city. Some firms also hope that sharing premises with young start-ups will expose their employees to innovative ideas.

In spring, when fine dust sweeps across the Korean peninsula, sales of protective masks surge. Convenience stores and pharmacies now monitor air-quality forecasts and stockpile extra masks before a hazy day arrives. Store managers report that sales often begin to climb a day in advance, as soon as warnings appear on the news and on smartphone apps, even while the sky remains clear. For many shoppers, then, the decision to purchase a mask hinges less on what they observe outdoors than on ____.

____. South Korea recently replaced the familiar sell-by date on most packaged foods with a use-by date. A sell-by date tells retailers how long they may display a product, and it is typically set well before the food actually spoils. Many consumers, however, interpreted it as the last safe day for consumption and discarded perfectly edible food. A use-by date instead indicates how long food can be safely eaten if stored as directed, so it falls later. The government hopes the change will curtail both household waste and expenses.

Beneath a forest floor, the roots of most trees are enveloped in fine filaments of fungi. These fungi extend far through the soil, absorbing water and minerals such as phosphorus that roots cannot readily reach, and transfer them to the trees. ____, the trees supply the fungi with sugars synthesized through photosynthesis, which the fungi cannot produce on their own. Some scientists contend that these fungal networks also connect neighboring trees, allowing nutrients to flow from one tree to another, although the extent of this exchange remains disputed.

Lightning originates inside towering storm clouds, where powerful updrafts carry water droplets high into freezing air. There, tiny ice crystals and heavier pellets of soft hail collide repeatedly, and these collisions transfer electric charge between them. The light ice crystals, which tend to acquire a positive charge, are swept to the top of the cloud, while the heavier, negatively charged pellets accumulate near the bottom. ____, the cloud becomes partitioned into regions of opposite charge. When the imbalance grows sufficiently large, the air can no longer act as an insulator, and a colossal spark discharges across the gap.

In East Asian calligraphy, the brush, ink, paper, and inkstone are collectively known as the Four Treasures of the Study. (a) The brush, usually fashioned from animal hair, lets the writer modulate a stroke's thickness through subtle shifts in pressure. (b) Ink traditionally came in solid sticks of soot and animal glue, which had to be ground on the inkstone with water. (c) Paper made from plant fibers absorbs ink almost instantly, so a calligrapher has scant opportunity to rectify a careless stroke. (d) Many contemporary students, however, now learn to write characters by typing them on computer keyboards.

Teenagers who work part-time are often unaware of the legal rights that protect them. (a) Under the legislation of many countries, they are entitled to at least the minimum wage, just like adult workers. (b) Employers are also usually obligated to provide a written contract that stipulates their hours and pay. (c) Many teenagers say that working at a café taught them how to deal courteously with demanding customers. (d) Because young workers are rarely acquainted with these regulations, some employers exploit them by withholding wages or demanding unpaid overtime.

When I relocated to Madrid for work, my Spanish was limited to ordering coffee. A colleague recommended a language exchange that convened every Thursday at a café near my office. The premise was simple: you spent half an hour conversing in Spanish with a local, then half an hour helping them with English. At first I was petrified of making mistakes, but my partners were patient because they were grappling with English themselves. After six months, I could chat with ease, and two of those partners have become my closest friends in the city.

Dear Ms. Reyes,
My parents insist that I study law, but I aspire to become a chef. Every time I broach the subject, we end up quarreling. What should I do?
— Torn in Toronto
Dear Torn,
Your parents are probably anxious about your financial security, not about cooking itself. Rather than arguing, demonstrate that you have thought it through. Research culinary programs, find out what chefs realistically earn, and perhaps take a part-time kitchen job to prove your commitment. Then invite your parents to sit down and discuss your plan. A coherent plan is far more persuasive than passion alone.

The Rosetta Stone, unearthed in Egypt by French soldiers in 1799, bears the same royal decree inscribed in three scripts: Egyptian hieroglyphs, a later cursive script called Demotic, and ancient Greek. Because scholars could already read Greek, the stone offered a key to the long-forgotten hieroglyphs. Even so, decipherment took more than two decades. Early researchers presumed that every hieroglyph symbolized an idea. The French scholar Jean-François Champollion demonstrated that many signs actually represented sounds, a breakthrough that finally rendered the script legible.

To many listeners, jazz improvisation sounds as though musicians are simply concocting melodies on the spot. In reality, improvisers rely on years of meticulous preparation. They memorize the chord progressions of standard tunes, rehearse countless short melodic patterns, and scrutinize recordings of earlier players note by note. During a performance, they combine and reshape this stored repertoire in response to their fellow musicians. Improvisation, in other words, is less like inventing a language from scratch and more like holding a spontaneous conversation in a language one already knows intimately.

Unmanned convenience stores, where customers scan and pay for items themselves, have proliferated in recent years. Owners save on labor costs, and shoppers enjoy round-the-clock access. Theft, however, has become a persistent headache. Although most stores are equipped with surveillance cameras, the footage is often reviewed only after losses are discovered, and petty thefts are rarely reported to the police because pursuing them costs more than the merchandise is worth. Some owners have begun requiring customers to scan a card or phone at the entrance before entering.

Many countries with aging populations face an intensifying debate over their public pension systems. As birth rates decline and life expectancy rises, fewer workers are paying contributions while more retirees are drawing benefits. Proposed remedies diverge sharply. Some economists favor raising contribution rates, arguing that today's workers must shoulder the burden. Others advocate raising the age at which benefits commence, noting that people now live and work longer. Younger workers, meanwhile, often resist both options, complaining that they are being asked to pay more for a system that may ultimately offer them less.

As veterinary care becomes more sophisticated, it has also become costlier, and a single surgery for a dog or cat can run to thousands of dollars. Pet insurance promises to alleviate that burden, but owners should scrutinize the fine print. Most policies exclude conditions the animal already had when coverage began, and many levy higher premiums as pets age. Routine expenses such as vaccinations and dental cleanings are often excluded as well. Experts recommend enrolling while a pet is still young and healthy.

Online secondhand marketplaces have made it effortless to sell unwanted items to strangers nearby. Unfortunately, they have also become fertile ground for fraud. A common ploy is for a seller to list a coveted gadget at an enticing price, ask the buyer to transfer money directly to a bank account, and then vanish without sending anything. Most platforms offer an escrow service that holds the buyer's payment until the item arrives, but scammers often persuade buyers to bypass it, claiming that the service is sluggish or charges extra fees.

Caffeine sustains alertness by blocking adenosine, a compound that accumulates in the brain during waking hours and induces drowsiness. When caffeine occupies the receptors to which adenosine normally binds, the signal to rest is muffled. Habitual coffee drinkers, however, face a dilemma. The brain compensates for daily caffeine by producing additional adenosine receptors, so the same cup yields a weaker effect over time. This is why heavy drinkers who abruptly quit often suffer headaches and fatigue: they are left with surplus receptors and no caffeine to block them.

New Caledonian crows, native to a group of islands in the South Pacific, are among the few animals known to manufacture their own tools. In the wild, they strip leaves from twigs and fashion them into hooks to extract insect larvae from crevices in decaying wood. Juvenile crows do not master this skill quickly; they spend many months practicing near their parents, often producing clumsy implements at first. Researchers have also observed that tool designs vary from one part of the islands to another, much as human customs differ between regions.

Slow Down to See More
For years, my vacations followed the same pattern: seven cities in ten days, a checklist of famous sights, and a camera roll crammed with landmarks I barely remember. Last spring I tried something different. I rented a modest apartment in a single coastal town in Portugal and stayed for three weeks. Without a packed itinerary, I began to notice details I had always rushed past. I learned the baker's name, discovered which beach the locals preferred, and spent whole afternoons reading in the same café. By the end, the town felt less like a destination and more like a temporary home.
This approach, often dubbed slow travel, is not for everyone. It demands more vacation days than many workers have, and some travelers simply relish the thrill of constant motion. But for those who can manage it, lingering longer in fewer places offers something a whirlwind tour cannot: the chance to inhabit a place rather than merely visit it. I came home with fewer photos, but far more vivid memories.

The ancient Olympic Games were held every four years at Olympia, a sanctuary in southern Greece dedicated to Zeus. Unlike the modern Games, they were as much a religious festival as a sporting event; animal sacrifices and offerings to the deities took place alongside the competitions. According to tradition, the earliest Games featured just one event, a sprint of roughly 200 meters called the stadion. Later, wrestling, boxing, chariot racing, and the pentathlon were incorporated.
Only freeborn Greek men were eligible to compete, and married women were generally prohibited from spectating. To ensure that athletes and spectators could reach Olympia safely, a sacred truce was proclaimed before each festival, allowing pilgrims to traverse warring territories unharmed. Victors did not receive gold medals. Instead, they were crowned with a wreath of olive leaves. Back home, however, a champion might be rewarded with free meals, statues erected in his honor, and enduring renown.

For more than a decade, large supermarkets in South Korea have been required to close two days a month, usually on Sundays. The regulation was introduced to protect traditional markets and small neighborhood shops, which struggled to compete with giant retailers. Proponents argue that the closures give small merchants a fair chance and guarantee rest days for supermarket employees.
Critics, however, question whether the policy is achieving its aims. Surveys suggest that on closing days, many shoppers do not head to traditional markets at all; they simply shop at the supermarket the day before or order groceries online. Meanwhile, farmers and small suppliers who distribute their products through supermarkets forfeit a day of sales. Online retailers, which face no such restrictions, have emerged as the clearest beneficiaries.
In response, several local governments have shifted closing days from Sundays to weekdays, a change welcomed by many consumers but opposed by some labor unions, who contend that workers deserve to spend weekends with their families. The controversy illustrates how difficult it is to protect one group without inadvertently harming another.

Free Wi-Fi is now available almost everywhere, from cafés and airports to subway cars. For travelers and students without generous data plans, it is a convenience that is hard to resist. Cybersecurity experts, however, warn that public networks carry genuine risks.
The principal danger is that many public networks do not encrypt the data traversing them. On such a network, a person with rudimentary software can sometimes intercept information transmitted by other users. A more cunning trick is the counterfeit hotspot: a criminal sets up a network with a name like "Free_Airport_WiFi," and unsuspecting users connect to it, routing everything they do straight through the criminal's device.
Experts recommend a few basic precautions. Users should refrain from logging into bank accounts or entering card numbers on public networks, and they should verify the exact network name with staff before connecting. Disabling the setting that makes a phone join open networks automatically also helps. For people who rely on public Wi-Fi frequently, a virtual private network, or VPN, which encrypts all traffic, offers more robust protection.

In April 2019, astronomers unveiled the first image ever captured of a black hole. It depicted a dark central region encircled by a lopsided ring of glowing gas, situated at the heart of a giant galaxy known as M87.
Obtaining the picture was a remarkable feat, because black holes themselves emit no light. What the image reveals is the black hole's shadow, silhouetted against superheated material swirling around it. The black hole is also extraordinarily distant, so it appears minuscule from Earth, and no single telescope was powerful enough to resolve it. Instead, scientists linked radio telescopes at observatories around the world, meticulously synchronizing their observations so that collectively they functioned like one telescope nearly as wide as the planet itself. The data were so voluminous that they were shipped on hard drives rather than transmitted over the internet.
The image also served as a test of Einstein's theory of general relativity, which predicted the size and shape of such a shadow. The results corroborated those predictions remarkably well.

훼손이 심해 흐려진 글씨를 겨우 '해독할(decipher)' 수 있었다는 뜻이에요. obliterate(완전히 지우다)·fabricate(꾸며 내다)·reiterate(되풀이하다)는 학자가 옛 글을 읽는 일과 맞지 않아요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
The senator tried to ____ the scandal by claiming the documents had been taken out of context.
문서가 맥락에서 벗어났다고 주장한 건 추문을 '대수롭지 않게 보이게 하려는(downplay)' 것이에요. corroborate(뒷받침하다)·commemorate(기념하다)·ostracize(따돌리다)는 의원이 자기 추문에 할 일이 아니에요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
Despite its ____ appearance, the plant is highly toxic and should be kept away from pets.
'겉모습과 달리(Despite) 독성이 강하다'는 흐름이라 겉보기엔 '해롭지 않은(innocuous)'이 맞아요. grotesque(기괴한)·cumbersome(거추장스러운)·ostentatious(과시하는)는 독성과 반대되는 겉모습이 아니에요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
Investors grew nervous when the company failed to ____ its claims of record profits with any financial records.
재무 기록으로 사상 최대 이익 주장을 '입증하지(substantiate)' 못해 투자자들이 불안해했어요. relinquish(포기하다)·disparage(깎아내리다)·conciliate(달래다)는 with any financial records 와 이어지지 않아요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
The professor's lectures are ____ of ideas borrowed from philosophy, economics, and biology.
세 분야에서 빌려 온 생각을 섞은 것이니 '혼합물(amalgams)'이 맞아요. reprisals(보복)·impasses(교착 상태)·stipends(급료)는 of ideas 와 어울려 이 뜻을 만들지 못해요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
The coach refused to ____ any rule-breaking, benching even his best player for arriving late.
지각한 최고 선수까지 뺐으니 규칙 위반을 '눈감아 주기(condone)'를 거부한 거예요. censure(비난하다)·abhor(혐오하다)는 거부하면 뒤 행동과 반대가 되고, rescind(철회하다)는 위반을 목적어로 쓰지 않아요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
The documentary attempts to ____ the myth that sharks routinely hunt humans.
상어가 사람을 사냥한다는 잘못된 믿음을 '떨쳐 없애다(dispel)'가 맞아요. bequeath(유산으로 남기다)·emulate(본받다)·placate(달래다)는 myth 를 목적어로 이 뜻을 만들지 못해요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
Once a ____ fishing village, the town is now crowded with hotels and tourists all year round.
Once ~ now 대조라서 지금의 '붐빈다'와 반대인 '외딴, 한적한(secluded)'이 맞아요. boisterous(떠들썩한)·opulent(호화로운)·cosmopolitan(국제적인)은 지금 모습과 대조가 되지 않아요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
Rather than confront his critics directly, the minister chose to ____ their questions with vague, rambling answers.
정면으로 맞서지 않고 모호한 답으로 질문을 '받아넘겼다(parry)'는 뜻이에요. solicit(요청하다)·rectify(바로잡다)·embolden(대담하게 하다)은 질문을 피하는 행동이 아니에요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
A: Have you seen Kate lately?
B: No, I ____ her since she moved to Busan last spring.
since(~이후로)가 과거부터 지금까지를 말하니 현재완료 haven't seen 이 맞아요. 과거형·현재형은 since 와 함께 못 쓰고, 과거완료는 기준이 되는 과거 시점이 없어요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
A: Jake didn't show up for the budget negotiation this morning.
B: He ____ forgotten about it. He's never missed one before.
과거 일에 대한 강한 추측은 must have p.p.(~했음이 틀림없다)예요. should have p.p.는 '했어야 했다'는 후회, need have 는 부정문·의문문에만 쓰고, ought to 뒤에는 have 가 빠져 forgotten 을 받을 수 없어요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
A: Would you like some more coffee?
B: Just ____, please. Too much caffeine aggravates my insomnia.
coffee 는 셀 수 없는 명사라 a little(조금)이 맞아요. a few·many·few 는 셀 수 있는 복수 명사에 써요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
A: Who's the woman talking to the dean?
B: She's the author ____ memoir we read in class last month.
뒤의 memoir 가 '그 작가의' 회고록이니 소유격 관계대명사 whose 가 맞아요. who·whom·which 뒤에는 관사 없는 명사 memoir 가 바로 올 수 없어요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
A: Are you still considering the job offer in Seoul?
B: Yes, but I'm not used to ____ in such a crowded city.
be used to 의 to 는 전치사라 뒤에 동명사 living 이 와요. live·be living·have lived 는 동사원형 꼴이라 전치사 뒤에 못 써요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
A: Did you attend the symposium on climate policy?
B: No. If I ____ about it earlier, I would have gone.
주절이 would have gone 이니 과거 사실 반대인 가정법 과거완료, if 절은 had known 이에요. knew 는 현재 반대 가정, have known·would know 는 if 절 꼴이 아니에요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
A: Do you know ____?
B: I think the keynote lecture begins at seven.
what time does the lecture start
문장 안에 들어간 의문문(간접 의문문)은 '의문사 + 주어 + 동사' 순서라 what time the lecture starts 가 맞아요. does 를 앞에 둔 꼴이나 주어·동사 순서를 바꾼 꼴은 틀려요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
A: Why is the elevator out of service?
B: It ____ right now. The technicians expect it to be operational by noon.
엘리베이터는 '수리되는' 쪽이고 right now 가 진행을 나타내니 진행 수동태 is being repaired 예요. 나머지는 모두 능동태라 엘리베이터가 무언가를 고친다는 뜻이 돼요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
A: Should I bring an umbrella to the outdoor ceremony?
B: Yes, take one ____ it drizzles during the procession.
in case 는 '~할 경우에 대비해'라 우산을 챙기는 이유가 돼요. so that(~하도록)은 비가 오게 하려는 뜻, unless(~하지 않으면)는 반대 뜻, as if(마치 ~처럼)는 뜻이 맞지 않아요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
A: I've never been to Jeju Island.
B: ____ Let's plan a trip there together.
부정문에 '나도 그래'는 Neither + 조동사 + 주어로 도치한 Neither have I 예요. So have I 는 긍정문에 쓰고, Neither I have 는 도치가 안 됐고, Nor I haven't 는 부정이 겹쳐요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
____ in the late nineteenth century, the bridge is the oldest structure still standing in the city.
다리는 '지어진' 것이라 수동 분사구문 Built 가 맞아요. Building·Having built 는 다리가 무언가를 지었다는 능동 뜻이고, To build 는 목적을 나타내 뜻이 맞지 않아요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
The scholarship committee stipulated that every applicant ____ an official transcript by Friday.
stipulate(규정하다) 같은 요구 동사 뒤 that 절에는 (should) 동사원형을 써서 submit 이 맞아요. submits·submitted·will submit 은 이 자리에 쓰지 않아요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
The new subway line will make the commute ____ it is now.
배수 비교는 '배수사 + as 원급 as' 순서라 twice as fast as 예요. twice 를 as 사이나 뒤에 두거나 faster 와 as 를 섞은 꼴은 틀려요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
By the time the museum reopens next year, it ____ closed for nearly three years.
미래 시점(다시 문 여는 내년)까지 이어지는 기간이라 미래완료 will have been 이에요. has been 은 지금까지, had been 은 과거 기준이고, will be 는 기간(for nearly three years)의 누적을 나타내지 못해요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
Soaring rents have made ____ for young families to remain in gentrifying neighborhoods.
make + 가목적어 it + 형용사 + for ~ to 부정사 꼴이라 it difficult 순서예요. 형용사를 it 앞에 두거나 it 을 빼거나 that 을 쓰면 틀려요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
____ of the two candidates had held public office before, so both campaigned as political outsiders.
둘 중 어느 쪽도 공직 경험이 없어 둘 다 정치 신인으로 나섰다는 뜻이라 Neither 가 맞아요. None 은 셋 이상, No 는 of 를 바로 받지 못하고, Either 는 '둘 중 하나는 있었다'가 되어 뒤와 맞지 않아요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
The coastal town ____ the novelist spent her adolescence has changed beyond recognition.
spend her adolescence 는 이미 목적어를 갖춰 장소를 이어 줄 관계부사 where 가 맞아요. which·that 을 쓰려면 끝에 in 이 있어야 하고, what 은 선행사 town 과 함께 못 써요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
Only after the forensic investigation was completed ____ the full extent of the structural damage.
Only + 부사절이 문장 앞에 오면 주절이 도치되어 did + 주어 + 동사원형이 돼요. 그래서 did officials realize 예요. 나머지는 도치가 안 됐거나 순서가 잘못됐어요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
Visitors are asked to avoid ____ flash photography inside the gallery.
avoid 는 동명사를 목적어로 받아 avoid using 이에요. to use·use·used 는 avoid 뒤에 쓰지 않아요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
According to ornithologists, the number of migratory species visiting the wetland ____ doubled over the past decade.
주어 the number(~의 수)는 단수라 has 가 맞아요. have 는 복수형이고, are·is doubled 는 '두 배로 늘었다'는 완료 뜻이 되지 못해요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
It was ____ that the inaugural ceremony was relocated indoors.
such 는 'such + a + 형용사 + 명사' 순서라 such a cold day 예요. a 를 such 앞에 두거나 형용사를 a 앞에 둔 꼴은 틀려요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
The regional festival was postponed ____ mounting concerns about the approaching typhoon.
뒤에 명사구 mounting concerns 가 오고 '~ 때문에'라는 뜻이라 전치사 due to 가 맞아요. because·although 는 접속사라 절이 와야 하고, despite(~에도 불구하고)는 뜻이 반대예요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
Many residents were ____ by the sudden announcement that the city park would be privatized.
주민들이 발표에 '놀란' 쪽이고 by 가 있으니 과거분사 surprised 예요. surprising 은 놀라게 하는 쪽을 말하고, surprise·to surprise 는 were 뒤에서 수동 뜻을 만들지 못해요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
Volcanic ash grounded the flight, so the stranded passengers ____ wait at the terminal overnight.
과거 일에 대한 '~해야 했다'는 had to 예요. must 는 과거 사실에 쓰지 않고, should have 뒤에는 p.p.가 와야 하며, need 는 긍정문에서 동사원형을 바로 받지 않아요.

Choose the best answer for the blank.
The climate in Busan is milder than ____ of Seoul.
비교 대상이 '서울의 기후'이고 앞의 단수 명사 the climate 를 되받으니 that 이 맞아요. those 는 복수, it 은 of 수식을 받지 못하고, one 은 the 없이 of 구를 받지 않아요.
